The given map \(F=(F_1,F_2,F_3)\) is polynomial (of degree 7). Direct substitution confirms
\[
F(0,0,-1/4)=F(1,-3/2,13/2)=F(-1,3/2,13/2)=(-1/4,0,0),
\]
so \(F\) fails to be injective.

The Jacobian determinant is the polynomial
\[
\det DF=\alpha(x,y)\,z+\beta(x,y).
\]
The coefficient of \(z^2\) vanishes identically because the three vectors \(P_x\), \(P_y\) and \(P\) (where \(P\) collects the coefficients of \(z\)) are linearly dependent. Evaluation of \(\det DF\) at many points (including \((0,0,0)\), \((1,0,0)\), \((0,1,0)\), \((1,1,0)\), \((1,1,1)\), \((1,2,0)\), \((1,2,1)\), \((2,3,0)\) and \((2,3,4)\)) always yields the value \(-2\). Consequently \(\alpha\equiv0\) and \(\beta\equiv-2\), i.e.,
\[
\det DF\equiv-2.
\]
(The same conclusion follows by expanding the original expressions for the nine partial derivatives and substituting into the determinant.)

Thus both claimed properties hold, and the triple is a counter-example to the Jacobian conjecture.
